source.title: Measuring Sparse Autoencoder Feature Sensitivity
source.authors: Claire Tian; Katherine Tian; Nathan Hu

record.tranche_reason: The paper studies sensitivity of sparse-autoencoder features, not the stated claims about neurons or neuron poles. It discusses the distinction between neurons and learned SAE features but does not test the claim versions on neurons.
record.gate_note: The paper reports results on SAE-feature sensitivity, including failures to activate on generated text judged similar to activating examples. These are related findings, but the tested components are SAE features, not neurons; no claim version's required neuron result is measured.
record.test_reason: The study measures sensitivity of sparse-autoencoder features (learned dictionary directions) in Gemma 2 2B and Pythia-160M, not model neurons. No version's required measure is reported: no neuron-pole audit shares (V1, V2), no InceptionV1 analysis (V3), no tool/architecture effect on neuron interpretability (V4), no neuron-based attribution graphs (V5), and no test of whether neuron explanations predict neuron firing (V6, V7). The authors explicitly distinguish SAE features from neurons and leave neurons to future work. The SAE result is analogous to V6 (interpretable by activating examples yet failing to fire on similar text) but concerns a different kind of unit, so it goes under fits_no_version.
record.authors_conclusion: Essentially correct. The authors conclude that sensitivity is a new axis of SAE feature quality, distinct from interpretability, frequency and decoder similarity. Many interpretable features have poor sensitivity, and average sensitivity declines with SAE width across 7 variants. They also find that sensitivity rises with L0 at fixed width. They make no claim about neurons, beyond suggesting the method could be applied to thresholded neurons in future work.
record.recipe_differences: Measures SAE-feature sensitivity by prompting an LLM to generate text from activating examples and checking feature activation; it does not audit neuron poles or score neuron explanations.
record.method_sensitivity: The paper reports that sensitivity varies with SAE width and sparsity; at a fixed width, average sensitivity increases with sparsity. It also reports that shorter generated-text prefixes are associated with a higher failure proportion.

fits_no_version.finding: Among 1,347 GemmaScope SAE features (1M width, layer 12, Gemma 2 2B) with auto-interp ≥0.9, 82 had sensitivity ≤0.5 and 23 ≤0.2. Humans rated 79% of non-activating generated texts indistinguishable from activating examples (83% for true examples).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: SAE features that look interpretable from their activating examples often fail to fire on new text humans judge equivalent. This is an SAE-feature analogue of V6.

fits_no_version.finding: Average SAE-feature sensitivity falls with dictionary width: 0.92–0.94 at 65K vs 0.85–0.87 at 1M in GemmaScope. The same trend holds across 7 SAEBench architectures at L0≈80.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Wider sparse autoencoders yield features with lower average sensitivity.

record.problems: The sensitivity analysis is limited to features occurring at least 15 times in 2 million tokens and filters features that fail to activate on shortened examples, which the authors say may bias toward simpler features. The authors also note that results for SAEBench variants are noisier due to smaller sample sizes. Results concern SAE features, limiting relevance to neuron claims.
record.rows_left_out: The paper gives additional SAE architecture and model averages in Appendix B, Table 1, and plots further scaling and cutoff results in Figures 7–11. They are not separately catalogued because they concern SAE features rather than any tested neuron-claim version.

untested.parts: No Qwen3-32B neuron-pole audit or shares of one-job, two-job, or not-understood poles.
No neuron-pole shares in any model; model comparisons concern SAE features in Gemma 2 2B and Pythia-160M.
No InceptionV1 or vision neuron analysis; no test of pose, recursive generalization, or superposition.
No measure of neuron interpretability share against tools, architecture, or regularization.
No attribution graphs built from model neurons; no replacement-model or reconstruction-error comparison.
No test of whether neuron explanations from activating examples predict neuron firing on new text; analogous test done only on SAE features.
No simulation-based scoring of neuron explanations; auto-interp scores used are for SAE features.

record.verdict_notes: The study cites Bills et al. (an original source) only as the origin of the auto-interp pipeline. The relation 'discusses' with T6 is kept. One could argue T4, since it uses auto-interp scores as a tool, but those scores are for SAE features, not neurons. The filtering excludes 51–79% of GemmaScope features, biasing the analysis toward simpler features.

versions.untested_parts: No Qwen3-32B neuron-pole audit or shares of poles with one job, two related jobs, or not-yet-understood jobs.
No neuron-pole shares across models, dense versus mixture-of-experts models, or models up to trillions of parameters. The model and width comparisons are of SAEs, not neuron poles.
No InceptionV1 cat-and-car neuron analysis or test of pose, recursive generalization, or superposition.
No vision-neuron interpretability estimates or test of the proposed architecture, regularization, and tool explanations.
No attribution-graph test using a large model's own neurons, and no comparison with a replacement model or reconstruction error.
The paper tests sensitivity of SAE features using generated similar text, not whether explanations of neurons predict neuron activation on new text.
No automated scoring of neuron explanations by simulating neuron activations on new text. The sensitivity measure is for SAE features.

rows.value: Among 1,347 features with auto-interpretability scores ≥ 0.9, 82 had sensitivity ≤ 0.5 and 23 had sensitivity ≤ 0.2.
rows.note: The paper describes these as interpretable SAE features with poor sensitivity; this is not a neuron result.
